newsitem.title: FRANCE: France reaffirms hope for stability in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: France reaffirms hope for stability in Zaire.

text.p: France said on Friday it wanted peace and stability in Zaire but declined comment on ailing head of state Mobutu Sese Seko's decision to bow out of power while retaining the title of president.

But French Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin, speaking out during a parliamentary election campaign, said the developments in Zaire were "a symbol of the failure of France's Africa policies" and said the international community must now help assure democratic elections in Zaire.
"Contrary to what (conservative French President) Jacques Chirac says, I don't believe that democracy is a luxury reserved only for rich nations," Jospin said on France 2 television.
"I don't want to see a dictator leave, only to be replaced by a military leader," he said. "The Zairean people must be put in a position to choose their leader."
French Defence Minister Charles Millon, asked about Mobutu's decision on France 3 television, said France "has since the beginning of the crisis called for a peaceful solution".

"It wants a guarantee of Zaire's territorial integrity and the re-establishment of civil peace," Millon said. "Due to its size and prominence in Africa, stability in Zaire is crucial for stability in the entire region."

Asked how a shift in power to rebel leader Laurent Kabila from Mobutu would affect France, a former colonial power in Africa with extremely close and enduring political and economic ties to the continent, Millon responded:
"The problem is not to choose. The problem is to hope that, with democratic elections, a stable regime can be put in place which can help bring about growth in Zaire," he said.
Foreign Ministry officials had no comment on Mobutu's decision to step aside.
France clung to Mobutu in the current crisis long after other international powers criticised his resistance to democratic reforms.
Mobutu has spent much of his time in recent months recuperating from prostate cancer surgery at his palatial villa on the French Riviera as Kabila's soldiers marched on the capital Kinshasa.
Asked if Mobutu was expected to come to France after relinquishing power in Zaire, a Foreign Ministry spokesman said: "We have no information on Mr Mobutu's intentions."

Asked if Paris would allow Mobutu entry if he sought refuge here, the spokesman said: "This question cannot be addressed since it is entirely theoretical and based on whether he would want to come. In any case, he has other homes elsewhere."

Analysts said they presumed the French government would not be eager to have Mobutu come to France until after a May 25-June 1 parliamentary election for fear his presence might become an campaign issue.
France has long regarded Africa as part of its diplomatic backyard.
But Paris has been pushed onto the sidelines in the Zaire crisis due to its stubborn support for Mobutu.
